title: Ex 2.6 #9 · P ∧ Q vs ∼(∼P ∨ ∼Q)
prompt: Are $P \wedge Q$ and $\sim (\sim P \vee \sim Q)$ logically equivalent? Decide, and back up your answer with a truth table, a chain of known equivalences, or a row where the two statements differ.
answer_format: equivalent or not equivalent. Steps are optional: truth-table columns, rewrite steps, or a row like P = T, Q = F where the two statements differ.
hints: Apply DeMorgan's law to ∼(∼P ∨ ∼Q): the ∼ moves inside and ∨ turns into ∧.
Two negations cancel: ∼∼P means the same as P.
solution: By DeMorgan's law, $\sim (\sim P \vee \sim Q) = (\sim \sim P) \wedge (\sim \sim Q)$.
Double negations cancel, so this is $P \wedge Q$.
So the statements are logically equivalent. (Both columns are T F F F.)

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses logical equivalence (Section 2.6).

steps.content: P ∧ Q : T F F F
